'''Walter Alvarez''' (born October 3, 1940) is an American professor in the Earth and [[Planetary symbols|Planetary]] Science department at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He and his father, [[Nobel Prize]]–winning [[physicist]] [[Luis Walter Alvarez|Luis Alvarez]], developed the theory that [[dinosaur]]s were killed by an [[asteroid]] impact.

==Biography==
Born in [[Berkeley, California]], Alvarez is the son of [[Luis Walter Alvarez]], a [[Nobel Prize]]-winner in physics, and Geraldine Smithwick. His grandfather was physician [[Walter C. Alvarez]] and his great-grandfather, Spanish-born [[Luis F. Alvarez]], worked as a doctor in [[Hawaii]] and developed a method for the better diagnosis of macular [[leprosy]]. His great-aunt [[Mabel Alvarez]] was an artist and oil painter from [[California]].<ref name=alvarezbioatberkeley>{{cite web|title=Walter Alvarez|url=http://eps.berkeley.edu/people/walter-alvarez|publisher=Department of Earth and Planatery Science at UCB|access-date=9 February 2014}}</ref>

Alvarez earned his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in [[geology]] in 1962 from [[Carleton College]] in [[Minnesota]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in geology from [[Princeton University]] in 1967. He worked for American Overseas Petroleum Limited in the [[Netherlands]], and in [[Libya]] at the time of [[Muammar al-Gaddafi|Colonel Gaddafi]]'s revolution.  Having developed a side interest in [[archaeological geology]], he left the oil company and spent some time in [[Italy]], studying the Roman [[volcano|volcanics]] and their influence on patterns of settlement in [[Ancient Rome|early Roman]] times.<ref name=alvarezbioatberkeley/>

Alvarez then moved to [[Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory|Lamont–Doherty Geological Observatory]] of [[Columbia University]], and began studying the Mediterranean tectonics in the light of the new theory of [[plate tectonics]].  His work on tectonic [[paleomagnetism]] in Italy led to a study of the [[geomagnetic reversal]]s recorded in Italian deep-sea [[limestone]]s. Alvarez and his colleagues were able to date the reversals for an interval of more than 100 million years of the Earth's history by using [[Foraminifera]] [[biostratigraphy]].<ref name=alvarezbioatberkeley/><ref name=historicalrecordlimestones>{{cite web|last=Alvarez|first=Walter|title=The historical record in the Scaglia limestone at Gubbio: magnetic reversals and the Cretaceous-Tertiary mass extinction|url=http://usm.maine.edu/sites/default/files/The%20Collaborative%20of%20Global%20and%20Big%20History/Alvarez,%20145%20Gubbio%20review%20Sedgy%202009.pdf|publisher=Sedimentology|access-date=10 February 2014|archive-date=22 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140722014453/http://usm.maine.edu/sites/default/files/The%20Collaborative%20of%20Global%20and%20Big%20History/Alvarez,%20145%20Gubbio%20review%20Sedgy%202009.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Impact theory==
{{Main|Alvarez hypothesis}}

[[File:Walter Alvarez and Alessandro Montanari at K Pg (KT) Boundary at Bottaccione Gorge near Gubbio Italy.jpg|thumb|Walter Alvarez at the original site where he discovered the dinosaur extinction evidence near Gubbio, Italy.]]

Alvarez and his father [[Luis W. Alvarez]], together with [[Frank Asaro]] and [[Helen Vaughn Michel|Helen Michel]], discovered that a [[clay]] layer occurring right at the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary|Cretaceous–Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary]] was highly enriched in the element [[iridium]]. Since iridium enrichment is common in [[asteroid]]s, but very uncommon on the Earth, they postulated that the layer had been created by the [[impact event|impact]] of a large asteroid with the Earth, and that this impact was the likely cause of the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], which occurred 66 million years ago and was responsible for the elimination of 75% of all then-existent species, including all non-avian [[dinosaur]]s.<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/aso/databank/entries/do80di.html People and Discoveries: Alvarez finds evidence of dinosaur-killing asteroid, 1980],''[[PBS]]'' website, accessed April 17, 2011.</ref>

This iridium enrichment has now been observed in many other sites around the world. In addition, the [[Chicxulub crater]] off the northeast coast of the [[Yucatan Peninsula]] was identified and is now regarded as the definitive evidence of a large impact. Consequently, a majority of scientists now accept an impact scenario as the most likely cause for the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction.<ref name="Schulte10" >{{Cite journal | last = Schulte | first = Peter | author2 = Alegret, Laia |author3=Arenillas, Ignacio |author4=Arz, Jose A. |author5=Barton, Penny J. |author6=Bown, Paul R. |author7=Bralower, Timothy J. |author8=Christeson, Gail L. |author9=Claeys, Philippe |author10=Cockell, Charles S. |author11=Collins, Gareth S. |author12=Deutsch, Alexander |author13=Goldin, Tamara J. |author14=Goto, Kazuhisa |author15=Grajales-Nishimura, José M. |author16=Grieve, Richard A. F. |author17=Gulick, Sean P. S. |author18=Johnson, Kirk R. |author19=Kiessling, Wolfgang |author20=Koeberl, Christian |author21=Kring, David A. |author22=MacLeod, Kenneth G. |author23=[[Matsui, Takafumi]] |author24=Melosh, Jay |author25=Montanari, Alessandro |author26=Morgan, Joanna V.|author26-link= Joanna Morgan |author27=Neal, Clive R. |author28=Nichols, Douglas J. |author29=Norris, Richard D. |author30=Pierazzo, Elisabetta |author31=Ravizza, Greg |author32=Rebolledo-Vieyra, Mario |author33=Reimold, Wolf Uwe |author34=Robin, Eric |author35=Salge, Tobias |author36=Speijer, Robert P. |author37=Sweet, Arthur R. |author38=Urrutia-Fucugauchi, Jaime |author39=Vajda, Vivi |author40=Whalen, Michael T. |author41=Willumsen, Pi S.| title = The Chicxulub Asteroid Impact and Mass Extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 327 | issue = 5970 | pages = 1214–1218 | date = 5 March 2010 | url = http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/abstract/327/5970/1214 | doi = 10.1126/science.1177265  | access-date = 2010-03-08 | pmid = 20203042 | bibcode=2010Sci...327.1214S| s2cid = 2659741 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>  Alvarez's 1997 book, [[T. Rex and the Crater of Doom|''T. rex and the Crater of Doom'']], details the discovery of the event.

In addition to his interest in extinction events and impacts, Alvarez has contributed to the understanding of [[Mediterranean]] tectonics, [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] geology and [[archeology]], and the establishment of magnetostratigraphic correlations.<ref name=alvarezbioatberkeley/><ref name=historicalrecordlimestones/>

==Big History==
[[File:International Big History Association formed at Coldigioco, Italy.jpg|thumb|Alvarez helped to organize a meeting of [[Big History|Big Historians]] at the Geological Observatory at Coldigioco in Italy in 2010 which resulted in the establishment of the International Big History Association.]]

Alvarez began teaching a course in [[Big History]] at [[UC Berkeley]] in 2006 under the title "Big History: Cosmos, Earth, Life, Humanity."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://lsdiscovery.berkeley.edu/detail_archive.php?identity=372 |title=Letters and Science Discovery Courses<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2011-05-22 |archive-date=2011-08-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110820081312/http://lsdiscovery.berkeley.edu/detail_archive.php?identity=372 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He last taught the course in 2011 where it was videotaped and made freely available online.<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL6PAzUorozDOGdGf7mW2llqZdxpI_ehib Walter Alvarez Big History course on YouTube]</ref> According to Alvarez, Big History is the "attempt to understand, in a unified and interdisciplinary way, the history of the Cosmos, Earth, Life and Humanity." This definition was later adopted by the [[International Big History Association]] (IBHA).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www90.homepage.villanova.edu/lowell.gustafson/bighistory/index.html |title=International Big History Association (IBHA)<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2011-05-22 |archive-date=2011-07-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724072220/http://www90.homepage.villanova.edu/lowell.gustafson/bighistory/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Alvarez's course is open to all majors and grade levels and seeks to provide a broad understanding of the past, present and future.

Alvarez helped organize a meeting of Big Historians at the Geological Observatory at Coldigioco in Italy in 2010,<ref>[http://ibhanet.org/page-1252419 Origins of the International Big History Association]</ref> which resulted in the establishment of the International Big History Association. In 2011, the IBHA is a 501(c)3 non-profit organization.<ref>[http://ibhanet.org/Resources/Documents/IBHA_Articles_of_Incorporation.pdf International Big History Association Articles of Incorporation]</ref>

Alvarez was one of the founding members of the IBHA,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www90.homepage.villanova.edu/lowell.gustafson/bighistory/contacts.html |title=Contacts for the International Big History Association<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2011-05-22 |archive-date=2011-07-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724072210/http://www90.homepage.villanova.edu/lowell.gustafson/bighistory/contacts.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and served on the advisory board until August 7, 2014 when he stepped down at the 2014 IBHA conference held at [[Dominican University of California]].

===ChronoZoom===
[[File:Walter Alvarez at the 97th Annual Faculty Research Lectures, University of California Berkeley.jpg|thumb|Alvarez presented "Earth History in the Broadest Possible Context" at Chevron Auditorium on the UC Berkeley campus where ChronoZoom 2.0 was first publicly demonstrated in 2012.]]

In partnership with [[Microsoft Research]], Alvarez developed a zoomable timeline called [[ChronoZoom]],<ref>[http://research.microsoft.com/en-us/events/escience2010/abstracts.aspx#Visualizing-All-of-History Abstracts – Microsoft Research<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> which is a computer-graphical approach to visualizing and understanding time scales, and presenting vast quantities of historical information in a useful way.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://eps.berkeley.edu/~saekow/chronozoom/projectinformation/index.html |title=ChronoZoom Project Information<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2011-05-22 |archive-date=2022-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815214923/https://eps.berkeley.edu/~saekow/chronozoom/projectinformation/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> ChronoZoom was introduced at the 97th Annual Faculty Research Lecture at UC Berkeley.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.lib.berkeley.edu/eart.php/2010/05/12/chronozoom-debuts-at-uc-berkeley-faculty-research-lecture-series |title=ChronoZoom debuts at UC Berkeley Faculty Research Lecture Series |work=University of California Berkeley Library|publisher=The Regents of the University of California |access-date=29 May 2014}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==

Alvarez was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1983, and elected a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter A|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterA.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=17 April 2011}}</ref> He was awarded the 2006 [[Nevada Medal]], the 2008 [[Vetlesen Prize]],<ref>[http://www.earth.columbia.edu/articles/view/2287 Geologist Who Linked Cosmic Strike to Dinosaurs' Extinction Takes Top Prize; The Vetlesen, on Level with Nobel, Goes to Walter Alvarez], [[Columbia University]] Earth Institute, October 16, 2008</ref> and the [[Penrose Medal]] from the [[Geological Society of America]]. In 2005, he received the [[honorary degree|doctorate "Honoris Causa"]] in Geological Sciences from the [[University of Siena]], Italy.

Minor planet [[3581 Alvarez]] is named after him and his father, [[Luis Walter Alvarez]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007%2F978-3-540-29925-7_3580 |chapter=(3581) Alvarez |publisher=Springer |date=2003 |pages=301 |isbn=978-3-540-29925-7 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-29925-7_3580 |title=Dictionary of Minor Planet Names }}</ref>
